name: Varanasi
info: Varanasi, also called Benares or Kashi, is a city on the left bank of the Ganges in Uttar Pradesh, India, inhabited since about 800 BCE, holy to Hindus, Buddhists and Jains, and long a centre of learning.

facts.founded: In Hindu scriptures the city, under its name Kashi, was founded by Shiva. Excavations in 2014 found artefacts dating back to 800 BCE, and two sites near the city, Aktha and Ramnagar, yielded artefacts dating back to 1800 BCE.
facts.where: On the left, crescent-shaped bank of the Ganges in the south-eastern part of Uttar Pradesh, India, between the river's confluences with the Varuna and the Assi stream, 121 km downstream of Prayagraj.
facts.known: Hindu pilgrimage, death and mourning; the ghats on the Ganges; the Kashi Vishwanath Temple; Sarnath, where the Buddha first taught; the Bhakti poets Kabir, Ravidas and Tulsidas; Sanskrit learning and Banaras Hindu University; silk weaving
facts.today: Varanasi is a city and the headquarters of a district in Uttar Pradesh, India, and remains a place of pilgrimage for Hindus, Buddhists and Jains.

t: Varanasi was the centre of the Kingdom of Kashi in the time of the Buddha, who first taught at nearby Sarnath, and it became a city of Hindu pilgrimage whose ghats on the Ganges are used for bathing and cremation.

It was raided and ravaged in 1033 and 1194, sacked around 1567, and had temples destroyed on the order of Aurangzeb, and much of the present city was built in the 18th century under Maratha and Bhumihar patronage.

A line of rulers took the title Maharaja of Benares from 1740, the East India Company acquired the city in 1775, and its Sanskrit college of 1791 and Banaras Hindu University of 1916 continued its record as a centre of learning.
dyk: In the 1830s James Prinsep's census put the number of temples in the city at around 1000, according to the account Rev. M. A. Sherring published in 1868.

sections.origins:
Varanasi lies on the left bank of the Ganges in the middle of the Ganges valley, between two streams, the Varuna in the north and the Assi in the south, which traditional etymology links to the city's name. Its older name, Kashi, comes from a Sanskrit root meaning to shine. Excavations in 2014 found artefacts dating back to 800 BCE, and further excavations at Aktha and Ramnagar, two sites near the city, uncovered artefacts dating back to 1800 BCE, which supports the view that the area was inhabited by then. In the time of Gautama Buddha the city was part of the Kingdom of Kashi.

According to Hindu scriptures Varanasi was founded by Shiva. In the story told there, Shiva tore off one of the five heads of Brahma, and when he came to Varanasi carrying it the head dropped from his hand and disappeared into the ground, which is why the city is considered an extremely holy site. The Pandavas of the Mahabharata are said to have visited it to atone for their sins. It is regarded in Hindu tradition as one of the seven holy cities that can provide moksha, and Hindu texts call it by epithets such as Avimukta, never forsaken by Shiva.

Other traditions also hold it holy. According to the Buddhavamsa, a Buddhist text, it was the birthplace of the earlier Buddha Kassapa, and Jains believe that the Tirthankaras Suparshvanatha and Parshvanatha were born there.
sections.growth:
Varanasi was a centre of religious and artistic activity by the time of the Chinese traveller Xuanzang, who visited around 635 CE and recorded that the city extended for about 5 km along the western bank of the Ganges. He wrote that it had some 30 temples with about 30 monks. Its religious importance grew in the 8th century, when Adi Shankara established the worship of Shiva as an official sect of the city. Through the Middle Ages it remained a centre for intellectuals and theologians, and several major figures of the Bhakti movement were born there, among them Kabir, who was born in 1389, and Ravidas, a 15th-century reformer, mystic and poet.

Under Mughal rule Rajput nobles, most notably Raja Man Singh of the Kachwaha rulers of Amber, rebuilt temples and ghats, and the Raja of Jaipur established the Annapurna Mandir. Guru Nanak visited for Maha Shivaratri in 1507. Much of the modern city was built in the 18th century, financed especially by Maratha and Bhumihar rulers, and many of the ghats were built under Maratha patronage. In 1737 a Jantar Mantar observatory was built above the ghats. Rev. M. A. Sherring wrote in 1868 that a census by James Prinsep put the number of temples at around 1000 in the 1830s. The Varanasi Municipal Board was established in 1867.

Silk weaving, brocades with gold and silver thread, carpets and brassware were among the city's crafts, and weaving was typically done in the household.
sections.rulers:
In the first millennium BCE Kashi was a kingdom of its own. In the Middle Ages the city came under the rule of other powers. Chandradeva, founder of the Gahadavala dynasty, made Banaras a second capital in 1090. After the battle near Jamuna in 1194 the Ghurid conqueror Muizzuddin Muhammad Ghuri ravaged it. It later came under the Mughals.

The Kingdom of Benares was given official status by the Mughals in 1737. After the Benares zamindari estate became Banaras State, Balwant Singh of the Narayan dynasty declared himself Maharaja of Benares in 1740. His clan organisation, with as many as 100,000 men backing the Benares rajas, gave them an advantage against the Nawab of Oudh in the 1750s and 1760s, and an exhausting guerrilla war forced the Nawab to withdraw his main force. The region was ceded to the Benares State, a subordinate of the East India Company, in 1775, and the Company acquired Benares city by the Treaty of Faizabad.

The city became part of the Benares Division of the Ceded and Conquered Provinces in 1805, the North-Western Provinces in 1836 and the United Provinces in 1902. Benares became a princely state in 1911 with Ramnagar as its capital, though without jurisdiction over the city proper. The kings kept their position until Indian independence in 1947, and in 1949 Vibhuti Narayan Singh incorporated his territories into the United Provinces. Since 1950 the city has been part of the Republic of India's state of Uttar Pradesh.
sections.life:
The ghats, steps leading down the river bank to the water, were where pilgrims performed rituals. Varanasi has at least 84 of them, most used for bathing and for Hindu worship, and a few used only for cremation. The Manikarnika and Harishchandra ghats are where Hindus cremate their dead, and the Hindu genealogy registers are kept in the city. Many ghats are associated with Hindu legends. Hindus hold that Brahma created the Dashashwamedh Ghat, probably the oldest, to welcome Shiva.

The city was a place of many faiths. It had an estimated 23,000 temples, and the Kashi Vishwanath Temple, the Sankat Mochan Hanuman Temple and the Durga Temple were the most popular for worship. Muslim weavers settled at Alavipura after the clash of 1034 to 1035, and in the silk industry most weavers were Momin Ansari Muslims. Sarnath, 10 km to the north-east, is where the Buddha first taught the Dharma, and the Buddha is said to have named it as one of four places of pilgrimage for his followers. Guru Ravidass Janam Asthan, a religious centre of the Ravidassia religion, marks the birthplace of Ravidas.

The city was long a centre of learning. The physician Sushruta, the primary author of the Sushruta Samhita, is said to have lived and practised there in the 5th century BCE. Jonathan Duncan founded the Benares Sanskrit College in 1791, India's oldest Sanskrit college, and Annie Besant founded the Central Hindu College in 1898. The Benares gharana of tabla playing developed in the city, and Tulsidas wrote much of the Ramcharitmanas there.
sections.crises:
The first Turkic incursion came in 1033, when Ahmad Nialtagin, a subordinate of Mahmud Ghazni, raided the city. His forces plundered the markets and looted gold, silver, jewels and perfumes, but retreated by midday because of the threat of local resistance. Hindu temples were partially destroyed, and the damage was limited as the army stayed briefly. In 1034 to 1035 Malik Afzal Alavi led a section of the army of Syed Salar Masud to Varanasi and was defeated near the site of the Masjid-e-Ganj-e-Shahidan, possibly by local forces under the Kalachuri ruler Gangeyadeva.

In 1194 Muizzuddin Muhammad Ghuri defeated the forces of Jayachandra near Jamuna and then ravaged the city, and many temples were destroyed. Around 1567 the Mughal emperor Akbar sacked Varanasi on his march from Allahabad. In 1656 Aurangzeb ordered the destruction of many temples and the building of mosques, and the city experienced a temporary setback.

Two mosques stand where Hindu temples are said to have been. Accounts of the Gyanvapi Mosque hold that Aurangzeb built it in 1664 after destroying a Hindu temple, and that remains of that temple can be seen in its foundation, its columns and its rear. Accounts of the Alamgir Mosque hold that Aurangzeb built it in 1669 on the ruins of the Bindu Madhav temple. Many of the city's mosques are said to have been built from the components of destroyed Hindu shrines. The Kashi Vishwanath Temple was destroyed and rebuilt several times.
sections.legacy:
The Kashi Vishwanath Temple of Shiva stands on the Ganges, near the Gyanvapi Mosque, which Hindu accounts name as the temple's original site. The present temple was built in 1780 by Queen Ahilyabai Holkar of Indore, and its two pinnacles were covered in gold donated in 1839 by Ranjit Singh, the ruler of Punjab. Ramnagar Fort, built in the 18th century by Balwant Singh, holds the history of the kings of Benares and a museum. The Ramlila of Ramnagar, sponsored by the Kashi Naresh, was begun around 1830 by Udit Narayan Singh.

The city's writers and musicians include Kabir, Ravidas and Tulsidas, Premchand and the shehnai player Bismillah Khan. Its educational record continued with Banaras Hindu University, founded in 1916 by Annie Besant and Madan Mohan Malaviya as India's first modern residential university, and Kashi Vidyapith, established in 1921 in response to Mahatma Gandhi's non-cooperation movement. Mark Twain wrote in 1897 that Benares was older than history, older than tradition and older even than legend.

Varanasi is now a city of Uttar Pradesh. The urban agglomeration had a population of 1,435,113 at the 2011 census, and nearly 70 per cent of the people follow Hinduism, with Islam the largest minority. Sikhs, Jains, Buddhists and Christians also live there, and Sarnath remains a place of Buddhist pilgrimage.

summary: Varanasi, also called Kashi or Benares, is a city on the Ganges in Uttar Pradesh that Hindus, Buddhists and Jains hold holy. Inhabited by about 800 BCE, it was ravaged by successive conquerors and ruled by the Maharajas of Benares, and it remained a centre of learning.
references: Winand M. Callewaert, Banaras: vision of a living ancient tradition (Hemkunt Press, 2000)
Diana L. Eck, Banaras, City of Light (Columbia University Press, 1982)
Vidula Jayaswal, Ancient Varanasi: an archaeological perspective (excavations at Aktha) (Aryan Books International, 2009)
Medhasananda, Varanasi at the crossroads: a panoramic view of early modern Varanasi and the story of its transition (Ramakrishna Mission, Institute of Culture, 2002)
notes: SOURCES: only wp/varanasi.txt exists; no history article was available, so every fact is from the city's own article.

START: the article says excavations of 2014 found artefacts dating to 800 BCE, and Aktha and Ramnagar (nearby, not the city) to 1800 BCE; it also calls Varanasi one of the world's oldest continually inhabited cities. I used -800 with circa true and put 1800 BCE in facts.founded as the nearby sites.

MOSQUES AND TEMPLES (read first): the article states flatly that the Gyanvapi Mosque 'was built by Aurangzeb in 1664 CE, after destroying a Hindu temple' and that the Alamgiri Mosque was built in 1669 over the Bindu Madhav temple, and that 'many of these mosques were constructed from the components of the Hindu shrines'. It gives no Muslim-side or legal position at all (no mention of the ongoing disputes). I wrote these as what 'accounts hold' and 'are said to have been', giving no verdict; the editor may want a second source for the other side. The Kashi Vishwanath Temple: the article says the mosque 'is the original site of the temple'; I wrote 'Hindu accounts name as the temple's original site', which is my attribution, not the article's. The mosque is administered by the Anjuman Inthazamiya Masajid (left out).

AURANGZEB DATES: temples ordered destroyed in 1656; Gyanvapi 1664; Alamgir 1669; the article also gives Tavernier describing the Vindu Madhava temple in 1665, and says the Alamgir mosque was built on the 'ruins' of the temple of Beni Madhavrao Scindia (a Maratha who, by other dating, lived later: the article gives no date for him). I omitted the Scindia name and the Tavernier note to avoid an apparent contradiction.
AKBAR: 'In 1567 or thereabouts'; I wrote 'around 1567'. The article then says Raja Man Singh rebuilt temples and ghats.

XUANZANG: 'some 30 temples with about 30 monks' as the article has it (odd figures; left as given). He is said to have visited 'around 635 CE' in one place and 'in the 7th century' in another; the city 'extended for about 5 km along the western bank'.

1740 and 1737: 'Kingdom of Benares given official status by the Mughals in 1737'; 'Balwant Singh declared himself Maharaja of Benares in 1740'; the lead says the Benares Estate was established in 1740. The Treaty of Faizabad is named only in the lead (1775); the body says the region was ceded by the Nawab of Oudh to Benares State in 1775. I combined these without contradiction. The article states Benares Division 1805, NWP 1836, United Provinces 1902 and Uttar Pradesh 1950; and also 'Varanasi was ceded to the Union of India in 1947' and Vibhuti Narayan Singh incorporated in 1949. The article's phrase that the dynasty-governed area continued 'until Indian independence in 1947, during the reign of Vibhuti Narayan Singh' is as given.
JANTAR MANTAR: article says it was 'constructed in 1737' and also that Muhammad Shah ordered an observatory in the 18th century; I wrote only 'built in 1737'.
SUSHRUTA: the article says he 'lived in Varanasi ... sometime during the 5th century BCE'; I wrote 'is said to have'.
RAMLILA: 'Kashi Naresh Udit Narayan Singh started this tradition around 1830' as given (the date is oddly early for that ruler; left as the article has it).
MANIKARNIKA: the article gives the current ghat as built in 1302 and mentions Gupta-period inscriptions; left out for space.

LEFT OUT: tourism, the 2021 Kashi Vishwanath Corridor, the present politics (Modi), administration, police, economy figures, transport, sport, media, climate, pollution, the 2006 attack on the Sankat Mochan temple, the meat bans. The article's History ends with a 21st-century paragraph about a corridor project; not used.
POPULATION: 1,435,113 urban agglomeration, 2011 census (as the article gives, with the year); religion 'nearly 70%' Hinduism.

Hindu cremation, genealogy registers and the 'Mahasmasana' name are attributed to Hindu practice as the article states them; the myths (Shiva's founding, Brahma at Dashashwamedh) are given as what scripture or Hindus hold. The Buddha naming four pilgrimage places: the article says 'is mentioned by the Buddha'; I wrote 'is said to have named'.
